title: Math Symbols: Copy & Paste Mathematical Characters
meta_description: Browse and copy math symbols including operators, Greek letters, set theory, calculus, and superscript characters. Click any symbol to copy it instantly.
hero_tagline: Copy and paste mathematical Unicode characters: operators, Greek letters, set theory, calculus, and more. Click any symbol to copy it instantly.
intro: Mathematical symbols in Unicode make it easy to write equations, formulas, and scientific notation in plain text, no LaTeX or special software needed. These characters are supported in emails, social media, documents, and messaging apps. Browse by category and click any symbol to copy it.

sections.label: Basic Operators

sections.label: Set Theory & Logic

sections.label: Greek Letters (uppercase)
sections.intro: Uppercase Greek letters used as identifiers in mathematics, statistics, and engineering: e.g., Σ for summation, Δ for change, Ω for ohms.

sections.label: Calculus & Analysis
sections.intro: Integral, derivative, summation, and limit symbols for calculus notation. A copied ∫ is one line of plain text, so it fits notes, chats and quick answers; an integral with limits stacked above and below needs an equation editor or LaTeX (\int).

sections.label: Superscripts & Subscripts
sections.intro: Superscript and subscript digit characters for exponents and chemical formulas. For additional numeric styles, see the dedicated number symbols page.

sections.label: Roots & Radicals
sections.intro: The precomposed radical signs in Unicode: square root, cube root, and fourth root. For exponents, see the superscript numbers above.

sections.label: Infinity
sections.intro: The infinity sign and its Unicode variations: proportional, eternal, and the mathematical infinity forms. ∝ (U+221D) sits here because it looks like an open ∞, but it means "is proportional to" and is neither ∞ nor the Greek letter α.

sections.label: Geometry
sections.intro: Angle, right-angle, perpendicular and parallel signs for writing geometry in plain text, such as ∠ABC = 90° or AB ⊥ CD. Unicode has two perpendicular signs that look alike: ⊥ (UP TACK) is the one most text uses, and ⟂ (PERPENDICULAR) is the dedicated relation sign. The degree sign ° is not the ordinal indicator º, and the diameter sign ⌀ is not the empty set ∅ or the letter Ø. Congruent (≅) and similar (∼) are in the comparison section above.
